subject: ss-endocrinology
title: Hormone synthesis, receptors and signalling: core principles for NEET-PG

steps.tx: Hormones act through **receptors**, and where the receptor sits decides the speed and mechanism of action. Peptide hormones bind **G protein coupled receptors** on the cell surface, triggering second messengers such as cyclic AMP. Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipophilic and cross the membrane to bind intracellular **nuclear receptors**, which alter gene transcription. Ligand binding is the initiating event for every GPCR cascade, and the heterotrimeric G protein links the receptor to downstream effectors.

steps.tx: Thyroid hormone synthesis starts with iodide trapping by the **sodium-iodide symporter**. **Thyroid peroxidase** then oxidises iodide and organifies it onto tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin, forming MIT and DIT, which couple into T3 and T4. Peripheral conversion of T4 to the active T3 is done by **deiodinases** type I and II, so low free T3 with normal free T4 points towards peripheral conversion problems. Type III deiodinase inactivates hormone instead.

steps.tx: Thyroid hormone receptors are nuclear receptors. When **T3** binds, the receptor changes shape, releases **co-repressors** and recruits **co-activators**, which switches gene transcription on. Pituitary negative feedback is mainly mediated by the TR beta2 isoform, which suppresses TRH and TSH. TSH itself acts on a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP in follicular cells. Feedback failure at the hypothalamus or pituitary gives a central defect in the axis.

steps.tx: Binding protein and assay issues can mislead thyroid interpretation. In **thyroxine-binding globulin** deficiency, total T4 is low while free T4 stays normal, so the correct response is observation, not replacement. High-dose **biotin** interferes with many immunoassays, causing falsely low TSH and falsely high T4 and T3 in a euthyroid patient. Always check for biotin before diagnosing hyperthyroidism.

right.title: Biotin interference
points: Free T4 and T3 falsely high

steps.tx: In G protein signalling, a **GPCR** activates a Gs or Gi alpha subunit, which changes adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP levels. Protein kinase A is the main effector of cAMP. Disturbances of this pathway cause disease: activating **GNAS** mutations produce McCune-Albright syndrome, and GNAS loss of function produces pseudohypoparathyroidism. PDE4D and PRKAR1A variants produce acrodysostosis, where PKA signalling is disturbed downstream of the receptor.
